$comment: Shared table for HTTP byte-range parsing. Rust's parse_single_byte_range in crates/ruvyxa_dev_server/src/static_assets.rs and parseByteRange in packages/ruvyxa/runtime/serverless-handler.mjs both answer this file. `ruvyxa start` and a standalone/node deployment serve the same public/ directory, so a video that scrubs under one has to scrub under the other.
$kindNote: whole = ignore the Range and send the complete representation, which RFC 9110 allows for any range a server does not wish to honour. unsatisfiable = 416 with `Content-Range: bytes */<len>`. partial = 206 with an inclusive [start, end].

cases.why: one byte
the opening probe a media element makes before it will play anything
an interior span, end inclusive
open-ended runs to the last byte
a last-byte position past the end is clamped, not refused
a suffix is counted back from the end
a suffix longer than the file is the whole file
surrounding space is not part of the value
a start at the length names no byte
wholly past the end
a zero-length suffix names no byte
an end before the start
an empty file satisfies nothing
multi-range is answered whole rather than refused; multipart/byteranges is machinery no client of this server needs
an unknown unit is not a byte range
no dash at all
an unparsable first position
an unparsable last position
an empty header value
a signed position is not a range specifier — Rust's integer parser accepts the leading plus and JavaScript's does not, so both are held to digits only
exponent notation is a Number() spelling, not an HTTP one
hexadecimal is a Number() spelling, not an HTTP one
a position past any real file is still a position: refusing it as unparsable would send the whole file instead of a 416
a suffix past any real file is the whole file, as with any oversized suffix
